message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
## Summary of the study

The study recommends that Cabinet approve weekly food waste collection for all 52,000 households from April 2027. It rests on four claims:
- a six-month pilot showing similar participation in houses and flats, so one uniform service can be rolled out;
- projected tonnage of about 3,290 tonnes a year;
- treatment at Brookfield, the nearby anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, giving a disposal saving of £243,000;
- a net cost of about £490,000, fully covered by a provisional new-burdens allocation of £520,000.

## Verdict

The pilot design and most of the cost arithmetic are sound. But three of the study's central conclusions are contradicted by its own figures:
- participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses;
- the tonnage projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot data;
- Brookfield can take only about 60% of the projected tonnage.

Once corrected, the service is not shown to be fully funded. The study needs revising before Cabinet commits roughly £1 million to vehicles in December.

## 1. Participation in flats did not "hold up"

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**. Yet the text calls this "broadly similar," and both the recommendation and the author's summary rely on that reading to justify a uniform service.

The pilot shows the opposite. Flats need a different approach, such as communal containers, door-to-door engagement or extra communications. Low participation in flats is common, so this result isn't surprising, but the conclusion drawn from it needs reversing.

## 2. The tonnage projection uses the wrong participation rate

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and 64% appears nowhere in the data. The study's 3,290 tonnes does follow from 64%: 52,000 × 0.64 × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks ≈ 3,288 tonnes.

The district has the same housing mix as the pilot, about 20% flats, so the pilot rates can be applied directly by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg per week | Tonnes a year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | 57% | | **≈ 2,870** |

That is about 13% below the study's figure. A smaller point: the "All" row of Table 1 shows 1.9 kg per week, but the weighted average is 1.86 kg.

There are also two reasons the corrected figure may be on the high side:
- **Novelty.** Pilot households took part while the service was new and under observation, and participation often falls after launch.
- **Seasonality.** The pilot ran January to June, so it misses half the year, although food waste varies less with the seasons than garden waste.

## 3. Brookfield can't take most of the projected tonnage

Section 4 says Brookfield will offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. That covers only 55% of the study's projection, or about 63% of the corrected figure. The remaining 1,070 to 1,490 tonnes a year has no stated destination. The next nearest plant is 46 miles away, with an unknown gate fee and much higher haulage costs.

This affects both the savings and the author's description of treatment as "local." It is also the issue most likely to affect the service's legal compliance and cost, so it needs resolving before approval:
- What will happen to the extra tonnage, and at what cost?
- Will Brookfield's capacity actually increase in 2029, and on what terms?

## 4. The service is not shown to be fully funded

The cost lines themselves are correctly calculated: £990,000 over seven years is £141,400 a year, crews cost 12 × £34,000 = £408,000, and the total is £733,400.

The saving is a different matter.

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | Covered |
| Corrected tonnage (2,870 t, all at Brookfield) | £212,400 | **£521,000** | **£1,000 short** |
| Corrected tonnage, only 1,800 t at Brookfield | ≤ £133,200 plus unknown costs for the rest | **≥ £600,000** | **Short by £80,000 or more** |

Several costs are also missing, despite the author's claim that "every cost line is shown":
- **Cover for absence.** Six crews of two leave no relief staff for sickness, holidays or bank holidays.
- **Implementation.** The dedicated phone line and web page, recruitment and training, and delivering caddies to 52,000 homes are not costed.
- **Overheads.** Supervision, depot space and admin are not included.
- **Financing.** The £990,000 vehicle order is due in December 2026, but the funding is only "provisional." The paper should state what happens if the allocation is lower or arrives late.

## 5. A tight timetable

- **Vehicles.** They arrive in March, crews are trained on them in March, and collections start on 5 April. A short delivery delay would leave little or no time for training.
- **Recruitment.** Twelve operatives must be recruited from February, ready to start in April.
- **Missing steps.** Caddy procurement and the Brookfield contract don't appear in the timetable.
- **The legal deadline.** It's worth confirming that April 2027 sits within Thornbury's statutory deadline or an agreed transitional arrangement. The study says councils "are required" to introduce the service but gives no date.

## 6. What is sound

- **A well-designed pilot.** It covered 4,000 households across a deliberate mix of housing types and urban and village streets. It used real set-out and tonnage data rather than national averages.
- **Low contamination.** Under 2%, measured at the treatment plant itself.
- **A sound method for savings.** Comparing the actual incineration cost with a quoted gate fee is the right approach. The problem is only the tonnage it's applied to.
- **Correct vehicle and crew calculations.** The timetable is also rightly worked back from the vehicle lead time.
- **Positive resident feedback.** It's worth reporting the survey's response rate, since people who took part in the service are more likely to answer.

## 7. The author's description vs. the document

- **"Participation held up across houses and flats."** It was 66% against 21%.
- **"Based on how Thornbury residents actually behave."** The projection uses 64%, which isn't the pilot's figure.
- **"Treatment is local."** Only 1,800 tonnes a year is contracted locally.
- **"Fully covered" and "every cost line is shown."** Corrected, the net cost exceeds the allocation even before missing costs are added.

## Recommendations before Cabinet

1. Recalculate tonnage by housing type using the pilot rates, at about 2,870 tonnes. Add a sensitivity case for participation falling after launch.
2. Replace the uniform-service conclusion with a separate approach for flats, and cost it.
3. Find a treatment route for the tonnage above 1,800 tonnes a year, and include its gate fee and haulage cost.
4. Add the missing costs: relief staff, implementation, overheads and financing.
5. Restate the funding position. Show the gap, if any, against the £520,000 allocation, and what happens if that allocation is not confirmed before the vehicle order.
6. Add timetable contingency for vehicle delivery, and include caddy procurement and the Brookfield contract as milestones.

The service is required by law, so the question for Cabinet is less whether to go ahead than on what realistic basis. That basis shows a funding gap and a treatment-capacity gap that Cabinet should approve knowingly.

I can draft the corrected projection and funding table for the report, or the section on a separate approach for flats.
